title: Review, Integration and What Comes Next
lede: Connect state, decisions and iteration to classes, collections, exceptions and text I/O. Build and explain a small data pipeline, diagnose boundary bugs, and preview functional transformations without changing the core course requirements.

sections.title: Trace the foundation accurately
concepts: Use the state you can observe

Tracing means running a program on paper, one step at a time, and writing down the value of every variable after each step. It is slow, and that is the point: your head skips steps, paper does not.

For a loop, say in words what the accumulator means after each pass. In the example below, after each iteration passed is the number of passing marks in the processed prefix: the boxes already looked at, not the ones still to come. A sentence like that is a loop invariant. It is true before the loop (0 passes in 0 boxes), every pass keeps it true, so it is still true at the end, when the prefix is the whole array.

Stepimarks[i]marks[i] >= 50passed after
before the loop–––0
1049false0
2150true1
3285true2
loop test3–3 < 3 is false: stop2

Before you predict, state the index range (0 to marks.length - 1) and the boundary condition. Then choose inputs that sit on the boundary. Exactly 50 is the useful test, because it is the only kind of mark on which >= and > disagree.

The off-by-one that crashes

for (int i = 0; i <= marks.length; i++) runs one step too far: on the last pass it reads marks[3] of a 3-element array and Java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Python’s marks[3] raises IndexError. Python’s for mark in marks: and Java’s for-each loop avoid writing the bound at all, which is one fewer thing to get wrong.

“The most effective debugging tool is still careful thought, coupled with judiciously placed print statements.”

Brian W. Kernighan, UNIX for Beginners, 2nd edition, 1978 Portrait: Ben Lowe, 2012 · CC BY 2.0

A print statement is a trace table the computer writes for you. Print the state before and after each change, as the trace example in section 3 does, and compare it with the table you wrote by hand.
Separate mutation from rebinding

Every call copies values into the parameters. Java’s language specification says so directly: when a method is invoked, “the values of the actual argument expressions initialize newly created parameter variables” (JLS §8.4.1). When the value is a reference to an array or object, the caller’s variable and the parameter now hold two copies of the same reference, so both lead to the same object. The Python FAQ puts it this way: “arguments are passed by assignment in Python” (Programming FAQ).

From there, two very different things can happen:

  • Mutation changes the object: values.append(3), marks[0] = 50, student.setMark(60). Every name that refers to that object sees the change.
  • Rebinding (assigning to the name) points one name at a different value: values = [9], marks = new int[] {9};. Only that name moves. The caller’s variable still refers to the old object.
Operation in the functionJavaPythonDoes the caller see it?
change an elementmarks[0] = 50;values[0] = 50yes: same object
add an elementlist.add(3);values.append(3)yes
call a mutating methods.setMark(60);s.mark = 60yes
assign the parametermarks = new int[] {9};values = [9]no: only the local name moves
build a new list–values = values + [3]no: a new list, bound to the local name
extend in place–values += [3]yes: for a list, += changes it in place
“Java passes objects by reference” is not quite right

If it were true, a method could swap the caller’s two variables. It cannot: static void swap(int[] a, int[] b) { int[] t = a; a = b; b = t; } swaps only its own copies, and the caller sees nothing. Say instead: Java passes every argument by value, and the value of an object variable is a reference. Python works the same way, and so do the two diagrams above.
Strings and numbers never change

Some objects have no mutating operations at all. Java’s String and Integer, and Python’s str, int, float and tuple are immutable: once made, they never change. A method that looks as if it changes a string, such as name.toUpperCase() or name.strip(), builds and returns a new string. If you do not keep the result, it is gone.

Looks like a changeWhat really happensDo this instead
name.trim(); (Java)a new String is returned and thrown awayname = name.trim();
name.strip() (Python)a new str is returned and thrown awayname = name.strip()
count += 1 inside a functionrebinds the local name to a new numberreturn the new count
point[0] = 5 on a tupleTypeError: tuples cannot be changedbuild a new tuple

This is why a function can never change a caller’s number or string: the only thing it can do is rebind its own parameter. To get a new value out of a function, return it.

The line that does nothing

name.trim(); on a line of its own compiles and runs in Java with no warning, and name.strip() is just as silent in Python. The first extra example below shows it happen. When a string “did not change”, look for a result that was never assigned.
Copy when you need an independent list

Assignment never copies an object. After b = a (Python) or List<Integer> b = a; (Java) there is still one list with two names. When you need a list you can change without touching the original, make the copy yourself:

You wantJavaPython
a second name for the same listList<Integer> b = a;b = a
a new list, same elementsnew ArrayList<>(a)list(a) or a.copy() or a[:]
a new array, same elementsArrays.copyOf(arr, arr.length)–
a new list of changed elementsa loop (or stream) that fills a new list[x * 2 for x in a]

These copies are shallow: the new list holds the same element references. Copy a list of Student objects and both lists still share the students, so changing a mark through one list shows in the other. For numbers and strings it does not matter, because they never change.

Python’s shared default list

def add(x, items=[]): looks as if it starts with a fresh empty list on every call. It does not. “Default values are created exactly once, when the function is defined” (Python FAQ), so add(1) returns [1] and then add(2) returns [1, 2]. Use items=None and create the list inside the function. Exercise 4 asks you to repair exactly this.

media.alt: A round road sign with a red border showing the number 50, beside a two-lane country road lined with trees
media.caption: A 50 limit lets you drive at 50, but not above it: the boundary itself is on the allowed side. That is speed <= 50, not speed < 50. A pass mark works the same way: “50 or more passes” is mark >= 50. Marks of 49 and 85 get the same answer from >= and >, so only a test with exactly 50 can tell them apart.

media.alt: Two metal door keys on a split ring, lying on a yellow surface
media.lead: A key is not the flat.
media.caption: A variable that refers to a list is like a key: it opens the object, it is not the object. Give a friend a copy of your key (pass the reference to a function) and if they go in and repaint the kitchen, you come home to the new paint: that is mutation, seen through every key. If they swap their copy for a key to a different flat, your key still opens yours: that is rebinding. A function only ever holds a copy of the key, so it can repaint your flat but it can never swap the key in your pocket.

sections.title: Combine parsing, models and reports
concepts: Make each stage have a clear contract

Almost every program in this course has the same shape: read some text, turn it into data, check the data, keep it in objects, compute something and write a report. Real programs (a payroll, a bank statement, the system that stores your marks) have this shape too, just with more stages.

Give each stage one named job and a contract: what it accepts, what it produces, and how it fails.

StageIn → outFails whenJavaPython
readinput → one lineno lines leftreadLine() returns nullfor line in f: ends
splitline → fieldswrong number of fieldscheck parts.lengthcheck len(fields)
converttext → numbernot a numberNumberFormatExceptionValueError
validatenumber → accepted numberoutside 0..100throw new IllegalArgumentException(…)raise ValueError(…)
modelfields → objectnever, if the checks came firstnew Student(name, mark)Student(name, mark)
summariseobjects → numbersno records at alla loop that returns valuesa loop, or sum()
reportnumbers → text–String.format, printlnf-string, print

Passing one stage proves nothing about the next. Linh,abc splits into two fields perfectly and still fails to convert. Binh,120 converts to a number and still fails validation. That is why each check lives in its own stage, and why each stage needs its own bad input in a test.

A single function that reads, splits, converts, checks and prints all at once can only be tested as a whole, and when it gives a wrong total you cannot tell which job went wrong. Small stages with one job each can be tested one at a time, with one bad input per stage.

Python forgives spaces, Java does not

int(" 85") is 85 in Python, which ignores spaces around the digits. Java’s Integer.parseInt(" 85") throws NumberFormatException. Files typed by people often have a space after the comma, so in Java call trim() before you convert.
Choose an explicit error policy

Some rows will be bad. Decide in advance what happens to them, and write the decision down. There are two common policies, and the only code difference is where the try goes:

PolicyWhere the try sitsGood forRisk
report and continueinside the loop, around one rowmarks lists, surveys, logs: one bad row should not lose the restbad rows go unnoticed unless you report them
stop at the first faultaround the whole looppayments, settings files: half-processed input is worse than noneone typo stops everything
for line in lines:
    try:
        records.append(parse(line))
    except ValueError as error:
        rejected.append((line, error))

Whichever you choose, two rules hold. A rejected row never reaches the list of good records. And the summary counts that list, not the number of lines you tried to read. Report both numbers: “5 lines read, 2 stored, 3 rejected” lets a reader check that nothing went missing.

A real surname that looks like nothing

A rejection policy is only as good as its checks. The journalist Christopher Null really is called Null. In 2015 he wrote in Wired that most websites accept his name, but some send him back to the form saying “the last name field can’t be blank”, some say “null” is a reserved term, and some just crash. Somewhere in those programs a stage mixed up the text Null with no value at all. Check what a field means, not what it looks like, and test with awkward but valid rows as well as obviously bad ones. Christopher Null, Wired, 5 November 2015
Turn a row into an object early

Once a row has passed its checks, put it into an object straight away: a Student with a name and a mark (Weeks 5–6), not two parallel lists names[i] and marks[i] that you must keep in step by hand. Every later stage then works with students, and cannot pair Linh’s name with An’s mark by accident.

Better still, let the constructor guard its own rule. If new Student("Binh", 120) throws, then every Student that exists is valid, and no later stage needs to check the range again. That is the class invariant from Week 6, doing real work in a pipeline.

JavaPython
reject a bad value in the constructorthrow new IllegalArgumentException("mark out of range");raise ValueError("mark out of range")
stop fields changing laterprivate final int mark;by convention: self._mark and no setter
one handler for “not a number” and “out of range”catch (IllegalArgumentException e) also catches NumberFormatException, its subclassexcept ValueError catches both int("abc") and your own raise
Do not print inside the model

A Student constructor that prints “invalid mark” and carries on has hidden the problem: the bad object still exists. Throw instead, and let the caller choose the policy. It is the Week 11 rule again: a class that calculates should not also decide what the user sees.
Keep the report as its own stage

Compute first, format last. A summary method returns numbers (count, passes, average); a separate report method turns them into text. Then a test can check that the average is 67.5 without reading printed output, and a CSV report can sit next to the screen report without touching the calculation (Week 10).

The report must also survive the case nobody thinks of: no valid records at all.

With no recordsJavaPython
total / count, whole numbersArithmeticException: / by zeroZeroDivisionError
total / count, decimalsNaN, printed without complaintZeroDivisionError
largest markCollections.max throws NoSuchElementExceptionmax([]) raises ValueError
NaN is a quiet failure

In Java 0.0 / 0 is NaN (“not a number”), and a report will happily print Average: NaN. Decide the empty-input policy yourself (print “no valid records”, or return nothing) and test it. Exercise 5 is about exactly this decision.

sections.title: Test boundaries and explain causes
concepts: A test should distinguish a mistake

A test is a small program run on an input you chose, with the expected output written down before you run it. A good test is one that would fail if the code had a particular mistake. A test that passes whether or not the rule is right is evidence of nothing.

Most mistakes live at the edges, so choose inputs at the edges. For a marks program:

CaseExampleCatches
no dataan empty file, []division by zero, the largest of nothing
one item[50]loops that skip the first or the last element
exactly on the boundary50> written instead of >=
one each side49, 51a boundary moved by one
top of the range100, 101a missing or wrong upper check
duplicatestwo students called Ana dictionary that silently keeps only one
untidy texta blank line, Mai, 50split and convert stages that assume tidy input
no final newlineMai,50 as the last linecode that only counts lines ending in a newline

For a method that changes an object, check the state as well as the return value: after take(2) returns true, left() should be 0.

A bug that waited nine years

In June 2006 Joshua Bloch wrote that the binary search in Java’s own library had been broken, “lying in wait for nine years or so”. The faulty line was int mid = (low + high) / 2;. When low + high is larger than the biggest int, the sum overflows to a negative number. That only happens for arrays of about a billion (230) elements or more, so no ordinary test ever used one. The fix is int mid = low + ((high - low) / 2);. He found the same bug in the binary search that Jon Bentley had proved correct in Programming Pearls. (Python’s whole numbers never overflow; Java’s Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 is -2147483648.) Bloch, Google Research blog, 2 June 2006
Explain from input to consequence

Explaining code is not reading it aloud line by line. A good explanation names the state, condition or method call that matters, and connects it to what you can see. For a bug, use four steps:

  1. Counterexample. The smallest input that shows it: [50] with > prints 0, but 1 was expected.
  2. First wrong state. Trace it and find the first variable that differs from your expectation: after the first pass passed is 0, and should be 1.
  3. Cause and fix. Name the line and the rule it breaks: mark > 50 leaves out the boundary, but the rule says “50 or more”, so use >=.
  4. Predicted effect. Say what the counterexample will print now, then run it: 1.
Weak explanationStrong explanation
“Line 6 checks if the mark is greater than 50 and adds one to passed.”“With [50], passed stays 0 because 50 > 50 is false. The rule says 50 passes, so it needs >=; then it prints 1.”
“It crashes because of an error.”“The line Tuan has no comma, so parts[1] does not exist and Java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Check parts.length first.”
“The list changed by itself.”“change was given the caller’s list and appended to it: mutation through a shared reference.”

Everything after the first wrong state is a consequence. Fix the cause and the consequences disappear. Patch a consequence and the cause turns up somewhere else.
Error messages are evidence

A crash is good news: the program tells you what kind of problem it found and where. Java prints the exception type first, with the stack trace below it; Python prints the traceback first and the exception type on the last line (Week 1). Most crashes in this course are one of a handful:

JavaPythonUsually means
NumberFormatExceptionValueError from int()text that is not a number reached the convert stage
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, IndexOutOfBoundsExceptionIndexErroran index one past the end, or a missing field after split
NullPointerExceptionAttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute …a variable that never got an object, or a method that returned null / None
ArithmeticException: / by zeroZeroDivisionErroran average of no records
ConcurrentModificationException, usuallyno error, but elements are skippedremoving from a list while looping over it (Week 7)
FileNotFoundExceptionFileNotFoundErrora wrong file name, or the program runs in a different folder (Weeks 9–10)
No crash is not the same as correct

The bugs in the table announce themselves. A logic error, such as > for >=, prints a wrong answer quietly. Only a test with an expected value written down in advance catches it.

“Beware of bugs in the above code; I have only proved it correct, not tried it.”

Donald E. Knuth, closing line of a memo to Peter van Emde Boas, 29 March 1977 (Knuth’s FAQ)

Even a proof is no substitute for running the program on the boundary cases.

sections.title: Optional: functional ideas and streams
concepts: A new way to express a familiar traversal

Optional enrichment. Most loops you have written do one of three jobs. Functional programming gives each job a name:

JobNameAs a loopJava streamPython
keep some elementsfilterif (m >= 50) kept.add(m);.filter(m -> m >= 50)[m for m in marks if m >= 50]
change every elementmapout.add(m + 5);.map(m -> m + 5)[m + 5 for m in marks]
combine into one valuereducetotal += m;.reduce(0, (x, y) -> x + y)sum(marks)

The small functions passed in, like m -> m >= 50, are lambdas: functions with no name, written where they are used. Java writes parameter -> expression; Python writes lambda parameter: expression, although a comprehension usually reads better than map with a lambda.

Ed’s optional Beyond Programming 1 lessons introduce first-class functions, pure transformations and stream pipelines. None of it adds computing power: every pipeline can be written as the loop you already know.

“So now reduce(). This is actually the one I've always hated most, because, apart from a few examples involving + or *, almost every time I see a reduce() call with a non-trivial function argument, I need to grab pen and paper to diagram what's actually being fed into that function before I understand what the reduce() is supposed to do.”

Guido van Rossum, The fate of reduce() in Python 3000, 10 March 2005 Portrait: Photograph by Daniel Stroud , first retouched version uploaded by User:Deedub1983 , second retouching by User:HarJIT ., 2014 · CC BY-SA 4.0

Python 3 moved reduce out of the built-ins into the functools module. For totals, use sum(); for anything harder, a loop is often the clearer choice.
Pure functions build a new result

A pure function computes its result only from its arguments and changes nothing else: it does not mutate its arguments, print, or touch variables outside itself. doubled(source) in the example below is pure: it builds a fresh list, and source is the same afterwards. Call it twice with the same input and you get the same answer twice.

PureNot pureWhy it matters
return [v * 2 for v in values]for i in range(len(values)): values[i] *= 2the caller’s list survives (1.2)
return totalprint(total)a test can check a returned value (3.1)
.filter(m -> m >= 50)a lambda that adds to an outside listthe Java stream rules forbid it

The Java documentation for streams says the functions you pass in “must be non-interfering, and in most cases must be stateless” (java.util.stream): they must not change the source list, and should not depend on anything that changes while the stream runs.

Java 8 on this site

The Java examples use Arrays.asList and collect(Collectors.toList()), which work in Java 8. Newer code often uses List.of (Java 9) and Stream.toList() (Java 16), which this site’s Java 8 compiler would reject. This section is optional; current Canvas instructions decide what is assessed.
Lazy pipelines run only when asked

A stream pipeline has intermediate operations (filter, map) that only describe work, and one terminal operation (sum, count, collect) that makes it happen. Until the terminal operation runs, nothing runs at all. The second extra below prints from inside a filter to prove it.

A stream can be used only once: a second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException. Python’s map, filter and generator expressions are lazy in the same way, and once used up they simply produce nothing more.

Java streamPython map / filter / generator
when does the work happen?at the terminal operationwhen something asks for values: list(), sum(), a for loop
use it a second timeIllegalStateExceptionno error, but no values: [], 0
keep the resultscollect(Collectors.toList())list(…)
The empty second list

bonus = map(lambda m: m + 5, marks), then list(bonus) gives the values and a second list(bonus) gives [], with no error. If you need the results twice, turn them into a list once and keep the list.
Comprehensions in Python

A comprehension is Python’s compact way to build a collection from another: the loop, the condition and the new element in one expression. Read it from the for: “for each m in marks, if m >= 50, keep m + 5”.

BuildsComprehensionResult for marks = [49, 50, 85]
a list[m + 5 for m in marks if m >= 50][55, 90]
a set{m // 10 for m in marks}{4, 5, 8}
a dictionary{m: m >= 50 for m in marks}{49: False, 50: True, 85: True}
nothing yet (a generator)sum(m for m in marks if m >= 50)135

Java has no comprehension syntax; a stream with filter, map and collect plays the same role.

A comprehension is for building, not for doing

[print(m) for m in marks] prints the marks and also builds a useless list [None, None, None]. When the point is an effect (printing, appending, writing a file), write a plain for loop. And when a comprehension needs two conditions and a nested loop to fit on one line, the loop is easier to read.

media.caption: Panning for gold is a filter: swirl the pan, the sand washes out, and the heavy gold flecks stay. Weigh each fleck and you have a map; add the weights and you have a reduce. Everything about the final assessment itself (date, format, length, what you may bring and which topics are in scope) is set on Canvas. Read the current announcements there; nothing on this website replaces them. What this page can offer is a way to practise:

misc.title: Where filter, map and reduce came from
misc.html:
Filter, map and reduce are not new. The ideas in the optional section have a long history, and reached the two languages of this course decades apart.

1964

Programs joined like garden hose

Doug McIlroy writes a Bell Labs memo asking for ways of connecting programs “like garden hose”. Unix gets pipes in 1972 (see the box at the end of section 2). Source

1977

Can programming be liberated?

John Backus, who led the team that created FORTRAN, gives his ACM Turing Award lecture Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style?, arguing for programs built by combining functions rather than by changing variables one word at a time. It is published in Communications of the ACM in August 1978. Source

2000

List comprehensions arrive in Python

PEP 202 adds list comprehensions to Python 2.0: [m + 5 for m in marks if m >= 50]. Source

2004

MapReduce

Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat describe Google’s MapReduce, inspired, they write, by the map and reduce of Lisp and other functional languages (see the box at the end of section 4). Source

2005

“The fate of reduce()”

Guido van Rossum explains why he wants reduce out of Python’s built-ins. In Python 3 it lives in functools; map and filter stay, and return lazy iterators instead of lists. Source

2014

Lambdas and streams in Java

JDK 8 reaches general availability on 18 March 2014. Its driving feature is Project Lambda: lambda expressions and the java.util.stream API used in this section. Source
